plan.topic: Why a weakened plague strain turned deadly: iron overload (hereditary hemochromatosis) in the 2009 Chicago lab case (CDC MMWR)
plan.angle: Title: 'Plague and Iron: How a Weakened Strain May Have Caused a Fatal Case (CDC) #shorts'. Answer within 10 s: 'This 2009 lab strain was weakened: it lacks genes it uses to grab iron. CDC says the researcher's undiagnosed iron overload (hereditary hemochromatosis) might have supplied enough iron to overcome that defect.' Then CDC's findings: the exposure route was undetermined (a respiratory route could not be ruled out definitively), and close contacts got preventive antibiotics with no additional infections identified. Close: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC). Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Point viewers to L1. 170 words or fewer.
plan.working_title: Plague and Iron: Why a Weakened Strain Turned Deadly (CDC) #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1. It teases the surprising iron detail and sends viewers to the full case-study video. | fact-check: The science is verified in the same MMWR (mm6007a1): a pgm- KIM D27 strain with iron-acquisition defects, and hemochromatosis that 'might have provided' enough iron. The working title 'Why a Weakened Strain Turned Deadly' states a cause outright, which MMWR only hedges. That is the causal-title problem that held S2 09-30. 'Turned deadly' also suggests the strain changed. The strain stayed attenuated; the host's iron overload is the proposed factor. Keep the respiratory-route caveat if the route comes up. Don't name the person and don't draw any link to Irkutsk.

package.title: Plague Lab Death 2009: The Iron Clue (CDC) #shorts
package.description:
In 2009, a weakened Yersinia pestis lab strain was linked to a Chicago researcher's death. Testing after death found hereditary hemochromatosis; CDC says iron overload conceivably might have helped compensate for the strain's iron-acquisition defects. One rare lab case; CDC says the exposure route remains unclear.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Have hemochromatosis? Talk to your doctor. Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

social.instagram_caption:
A weakened plague strain was linked to a researcher's death in 2009. CDC says iron overload conceivably might have helped. This was one rare lab case.

In 2009, a Chicago researcher died after lab exposure to an attenuated (weakened) Yersinia pestis strain (CDC, MMWR 2011).

The strain has defects in how it grabs iron, which is part of why it's attenuated and far less able to cause disease.

After the researcher died, testing found hereditary hemochromatosis, an inherited condition that causes iron overload.

CDC says the extra iron conceivably might have helped compensate for the strain's iron-acquisition defect.

CDC says the exposure route remains unclear. Findings fit septicemic plague, not pneumonic, though a respiratory route couldn't be ruled out definitively.

All 30 coworkers were prescribed preventive antibiotics. 94% of other close contacts accepted them. No additional infections were identified.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every factual claim against the live sources, and they hold up. The CDC MMWR report (Vol 60 No 7, Feb 25, 2011) confirms these points:
- The KIM D27 strain is described as "attenuated" and has "defects in its ability to acquire iron".
- The 60-year-old researcher's hereditary hemochromatosis was found only through postmortem testing.
- The report's wording on iron is "Conceivably, hemochromatosis-induced iron overload might have a similar effect… compensating for its iron-acquisition defects".
- On the route, it says "the route of transmission for the infection remains unclear", the findings are "consistent with septicemic plague and inconsistent with pneumonic plague", and "a respiratory route of infection cannot be ruled out definitively".
- "All 30 coworkers were prescribed prophylaxis". Separately, 61 of 65 other close contacts (94%) accepted prophylaxis.
- "No additional Y. pestis infections have been identified".

The other sources also check out. CDC About Plague (updated Aug 24, 2026) has the exact sentence "Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly." CDC Signs and Symptoms of Plague (updated May 15, 2024) lists fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain for pneumonic plague. The NIDDK Hemochromatosis page (last reviewed January 2020) supports the "inherited iron overload" gloss.

The framing matches the evidence. The script says "linked to", keeps "conceivably… might have", and never says "caused". The rare-case caveat and the hemochromatosis "talk to your doctor" line are there, as are the urgent-contact line and the exact "If you're worried, talk to a health professional." line. The piece is clearly historical and makes no claims about the current Irkutsk case. There are only minor fixes: the title says "Why" when the iron explanation is a hedged hypothesis, the narration is 1 word over the 170-word cap, and the s1 card wording is a little ambiguous.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right at the top of the target window (-13.5 dB under voice) so left untouched; it already has room to breathe in the one real pause. The auto cue list badly over-stacked several moments (5-7 effects within ~1-1.5s at 4.2s, 12.8-14s, 20.6-21.8s, 40.3-41.4s, 51.3-53s and the chips/urgent beats near 64-70s) and included redundant simultaneous duplicates (two transition sounds, two bubbles, two swooshes at the same timestamp); I dropped the redundant layers and kept at most 3 per cluster, favoring the cleaner accent (hit/pop/ding) over generic swoosh/whoosh stacking. I nudged the stat-reveal dings (30 and 94%) and the mid-cluster bubble near the "iron overload" headline up slightly so key numeric reveals land as a felt accent rather than disappearing under speech. Added five bespoke cues (somber pulse on the opening fatal-case line, sterile lab hum under the hemochromatosis label, a restrained tension riser on the iron-overload reveal, a warm resolving chime on "no additional infections," and a brief soft urgent tone on "act urgently") to carry emotional weight the stock kit can't, all kept well under the voice.
